capsules.front_content: We have all seen repository logs filled with commit messages like 'fixed stuff', 'asdf', or 'updates'. Six months later, when a production bug appears, nobody on the team knows which commit introduced the change or why. How do great engineers write commit messages?
capsules.back_content: A great commit message explains WHAT changed and WHY, not just how. Follow the conventional standard: a concise imperative summary line under 50 characters (e.g., 'fix: resolve race condition in token refresh'), followed by an optional blank line and paragraph explaining the context. Writing in the imperative mood ('Add feature' rather than 'Added feature') matches Git's internal generated messages (like 'Merge branch'). Good commit messages are letters to your future self.

quiz.prompt: Which commit message follows professional software engineering best practices?
quiz.option_a: changes
quiz.option_b: fix: prevent divide-by-zero crash when progress percentage is calculated with zero capsules
quiz.option_c: I worked on the website today and fixed some files
quiz.option_d: WIP final final v2
quiz.explanation: It uses the conventional commit format, states the specific bug addressed in the imperative mood, and clarifies the problem solved.
quiz.kids_hint: Label the box clearly: 'Fixed leaky water bottle cap' instead of just 'stuff'!

capsules.title: Branching: Fearless Experimentation in Isolation
capsules.front_content: In traditional file folders, experimenting with a major new feature meant duplicating the entire folder: 'Project_Final_v2_TEST'. If you broke things, you had to manually merge changes back. Git branches eliminate this risk entirely. What is a Git branch under the hood?
capsules.back_content: In Git, a branch is not an expensive copy of all your files—it is an ultra-lightweight 41-byte text pointer pointing to a specific commit hash! When you create a branch ('git checkout -b feature/dark-mode'), Git simply creates a new pointer. As you commit on that branch, the pointer advances. Your main branch remains completely untouched and safe. If the experiment fails, deleting the branch takes 1 millisecond with zero risk to main.

quiz.prompt: What is a Git branch under the hood in Git's internal architecture?
quiz.option_a: A separate physical folder on your hard drive with duplicate files
quiz.option_b: A lightweight movable pointer to a specific commit hash
quiz.option_c: An encrypted password string
quiz.option_d: A remote server backup file
quiz.explanation: A Git branch is simply a named reference pointing to the tip of a commit lineage, making branch creation and switching instantaneous.
quiz.kids_hint: A branch is a bookmark in your book! You can put a second bookmark on page 20, read ahead to see what happens, and flip right back to your first bookmark anytime.

capsules.title: Merge Conflicts: Resolving Code Collisions
capsules.front_content: You and your teammate both edit line 14 of 'settings.py' on separate branches. You merge your branch, and then your teammate tries to merge theirs. Git pauses and outputs: 'CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in settings.py'. Don't panic! What is Git telling you?
capsules.back_content: A merge conflict occurs when two branches modify the exact same lines of code since their common ancestor, and Git cannot automatically know which human intention is correct. Git inserts conflict markers into the file: '<<<<<<< HEAD' shows your current branch changes, '=======' separates the versions, and '>>>>>>> branch' shows the incoming branch changes. To resolve it, open the file, decide the correct unified logic, delete the markers, and stage/commit the resolved file.

quiz.prompt: What should a developer do when encountering merge conflict markers ('<<<<<<<', '=======', '>>>>>>>') in a file?
quiz.option_a: Delete the entire file immediately
quiz.option_b: Manually edit the code to keep the intended unified logic, remove all conflict markers, stage the file, and commit
quiz.option_c: Restart the computer to let the operating system resolve it
quiz.option_d: Ignore the markers and push directly to production
quiz.explanation: Resolving a conflict requires human judgment: review both versions, integrate the correct code, remove Git's marker annotations, and finalize the commit.
quiz.kids_hint: Two painters painted the front door different colors! You sit down together, agree on the best color, wipe off the chalk marks, and paint it right.

capsules.title: Remotes: Push, Fetch & Pull Demystified
capsules.front_content: Your Git repository lives on your local laptop. GitHub (or GitLab) hosts a copy on the cloud called a Remote ('origin'). What is the subtle but vital difference between 'git fetch' and 'git pull' when synchronizing team changes?
capsules.back_content: 'git fetch' downloads new commits and branches from the remote repository to your local machine, updating remote-tracking pointers (like origin/main) without touching your current working files. It is completely safe. 'git pull', on the other hand, performs 'git fetch' followed immediately by 'git merge'. Professional developers often fetch first to inspect incoming changes ('git log origin/main') before deciding how and when to merge.

quiz.prompt: What does 'git fetch origin' do?
quiz.option_a: Overwrites your local working directory with the remote code immediately
quiz.option_b: Downloads new commits and branches from the remote without modifying your working files or current branch
quiz.option_c: Deletes the remote repository on GitHub
quiz.option_d: Creates a new pull request on GitHub
quiz.explanation: Fetch synchronizes your repository's knowledge of the remote state safely, without merging or touching your working directory files.
quiz.kids_hint: Fetch is picking up the mail from the mailbox and putting it on the hallway table to read whenever you're ready, without tearing open letters immediately!

capsules.title: Pull Requests & Peer Code Review
capsules.front_content: In professional software teams, developers almost never push code directly to the 'main' branch. Instead, all work flows through Pull Requests (PRs). Why has the Pull Request become the universal standard for collaborative software delivery?
capsules.back_content: A Pull Request is a formal proposal: 'Here is my feature branch; please review it and merge it into main.' PRs provide a dedicated forum for code review, where teammates spot edge-case bugs, suggest cleaner patterns, and verify test coverage before code reaches production. Automated CI/CD pipelines run unit tests and linters on the PR automatically. Code review spreads knowledge across the team and elevates quality.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary engineering purpose of a Pull Request (PR) in modern software teams?
quiz.option_a: To charge money for code contributions
quiz.option_b: To facilitate peer code review, discussions, and automated CI test checks before integrating changes into main
quiz.option_c: To convert Python code into JavaScript
quiz.option_d: To permanently delete historical commits
quiz.explanation: Pull requests provide a collaborative review checkpoint where humans review logic and automated tests validate correctness prior to merging.
quiz.kids_hint: A pull request is showing your completed group project poster to your teammate before handing it in to the teacher!

capsules.title: Rebase vs Merge: Maintaining Clean History
capsules.front_content: While you worked on your feature branch for three days, teammates merged 10 new commits into main. Now you need to bring your branch up to date. You have two options: 'git merge main' or 'git rebase main'. How do they differ?
capsules.back_content: 'git merge' creates a new 'merge commit' tying main and your branch together, preserving the exact non-linear chronology of when commits were authored. 'git rebase', however, replays your branch commits on top of the latest commit on main, creating a perfectly linear history as if you wrote your feature today. Rule of thumb: rebase local, unpushed feature branches for clean linear history; NEVER rebase public shared branches.

quiz.prompt: Why should you avoid running 'git rebase' on public shared branches (like main)?
quiz.option_a: Rebase creates duplicate files on your hard drive
quiz.option_b: Rebase rewrites commit hashes, which desynchronizes the history of other teammates collaborating on that branch
quiz.option_c: Rebase deletes all comments in your code
quiz.option_d: Git rebase requires a paid GitHub Enterprise plan
quiz.explanation: Rebasing creates new SHA-1 hashes for replayed commits. Rewriting shared history causes severe divergence for collaborators.
quiz.kids_hint: Never change the rules of a board game in the middle of a turn when all your friends are already playing!

capsules.title: Git Stash: Pausing Work Mid-Stream
capsules.front_content: You are halfway through refactoring a complex function. Your working directory is full of half-written code that doesn't even compile yet. Suddenly, your manager says: 'Production has an emergency bug on main; you need to fix it right now!' You cannot commit broken work, but you cannot lose your progress. What do you do?
capsules.back_content: Run 'git stash'. Git sweeps all your uncommitted modified files onto a temporary clipboard stack, returning your working directory to a clean, pristine state matching the last commit. You switch to main, fix the production bug, commit, and push. Then switch back to your feature branch and run 'git stash pop'—all your in-progress work reappears exactly where you left it! Stashing prevents messy commits.

quiz.prompt: What does 'git stash' do to your current working directory?
quiz.option_a: Deletes all files permanently
quiz.option_b: Temporarily saves your uncommitted modifications onto a stack and reverts your working directory to the clean HEAD commit
quiz.option_c: Pushes your uncommitted changes directly to GitHub
quiz.option_d: Renames your git branch to 'stash'
quiz.explanation: 'git stash' shelves uncommitted modifications so you can switch contexts cleanly, and 'git stash pop' restores them later.
quiz.kids_hint: It's like putting your half-finished puzzle into a safe drawer so you can clear the kitchen table for dinner, and taking it back out afterward!

capsules.title: Undoing Mistakes: Reset, Revert & The Reflog
capsules.front_content: Every developer has experienced that cold knot in the stomach after accidentally running a command that seemed to wipe out hours of work. But here is the secret that seasoned developers know: in Git, it is almost impossible to lose committed data. How does Git safeguard your history?
capsules.back_content: 'git revert <hash>' creates a new commit that safely reverses an old mistake without altering history (safe for shared branches). 'git reset' moves branch pointers locally. And if you accidentally delete a branch or reset to the wrong commit, Git's secret superpower is 'git reflog' (reference log): it records every movement of HEAD on your machine. You can find the lost commit hash in the reflog and restore it instantly.

quiz.prompt: How does 'git revert' differ from 'git reset' when undoing a past commit?
quiz.option_a: git revert deletes the repository, while git reset renames it
quiz.option_b: git revert creates a new commit that inverts the changes of a prior commit, safely preserving history on shared branches
quiz.option_c: git reset can only run on Windows, while git revert runs on Linux
quiz.option_d: There is no difference; they are aliases
quiz.explanation: 'git revert' is additive: it appends a new snapshot undoing changes, making it safe for public branches where history should not be altered.
quiz.kids_hint: git revert doesn't rip out the old diary page—it writes a new note saying 'I changed my mind about yesterday's idea'!

name: Data Structures & Algorithmic Thinking
description: Build strong algorithmic problem-solving skills with arrays, linked lists, trees, hash tables, and Big-O computational complexity.

capsules.title: Big-O Notation: Measuring Computational Efficiency
capsules.front_content: A developer writes an algorithm that runs in 0.01 seconds on their laptop with 10 test records. Deployed to production with 1,000,000 records, the server crashes. Measuring speed in seconds is misleading because hardware varies. How do computer scientists measure algorithm efficiency universally?
capsules.back_content: Big-O notation describes how execution time or memory space scales as input size (n) grows toward infinity. O(1) is constant time (instant, like hash table lookup). O(log n) is logarithmic (binary search). O(n) is linear (inspecting every item once). O(n^2) is quadratic (nested loops, which balloon exponentially). An O(n) algorithm might process 1,000,000 items in 1 second, while an O(n^2) algorithm takes 11 days on the same machine. Big-O is the language of scalability.

quiz.prompt: If an algorithm's execution time doubles each time the input size (n) doubles, what is its time complexity?
quiz.option_b: O(n) - Linear
quiz.option_c: O(n^2) - Quadratic
quiz.option_d: O(2^n) - Exponential
quiz.explanation: In an O(n) linear algorithm, time scales directly in linear proportion to input size: 2x data takes 2x time.
quiz.kids_hint: If reading 1 page takes 1 minute, reading 10 pages takes 10 minutes—that's linear time!

capsules.title: Dynamic Arrays & Contiguous Memory Allocation
capsules.front_content: In computer hardware, RAM is a vast street of numbered memory slots. When you create an array of 5 integers, the operating system allocates 5 contiguous slots in a row. What architectural superpower does contiguous memory give to arrays?
capsules.back_content: Contiguous memory enables Random Access in O(1) constant time. Because elements sit back-to-back, jumping to 'array[i]' requires only simple arithmetic: 'memory_address = base_address + (i * element_size)'. The CPU jumps directly to index 999 as fast as index 0. The trade-off: inserting or deleting at the beginning requires shifting all subsequent elements over, taking O(n) time. Dynamic arrays (like Python lists) double their allocated buffer when capacity fills.

quiz.prompt: Why is accessing an element by index in an array (e.g. array[45]) an O(1) constant-time operation?
quiz.option_a: Because the CPU guesses the answer randomly
quiz.option_b: Because contiguous memory allows the CPU to calculate the exact physical memory address with a single multiplication
quiz.option_c: Because arrays are stored on the hard drive
quiz.option_d: Because arrays contain zero numbers
quiz.explanation: Address arithmetic (start_address + index * size) computes the exact memory offset instantly without inspecting prior elements.
quiz.kids_hint: House #5 on a numbered street is right next to house #4! You don't have to knock on every door to find it.

capsules.title: Linked Lists: Pointer-Chained Dynamic Sequences
capsules.front_content: What if you cannot allocate a large chunk of contiguous memory because RAM is fragmented into small pockets? Or what if your application constantly inserts and removes elements from the very beginning of a sequence? Enter the Linked List.
capsules.back_content: A Linked List consists of separate Nodes scattered anywhere in memory. Each node holds data and a Pointer referencing the address of the next node. Inserting or deleting at the head takes O(1) constant time—you simply update a pointer! The trade-off: linked lists lose instant O(1) random index access. To find the 500th element, you must traverse node-by-node from the head in O(n) time. Singly linked lists point forward; doubly linked lists point both forward and backward.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary advantage of a Singly Linked List over a standard array?
quiz.option_a: Instant O(1) random index access to any element
quiz.option_b: Efficient O(1) insertion and deletion at the beginning without shifting existing elements
quiz.option_c: Uses zero pointer memory overhead
quiz.option_d: Automatic sorting of elements
quiz.explanation: Adding a node to the front of a linked list only requires updating the new node's next pointer and head pointer, an O(1) operation.
quiz.kids_hint: A treasure hunt where each clue tells you where the NEXT clue is hidden! You can easily slip a new clue between two others without moving the whole room.

capsules.title: Stacks: Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) Processing
capsules.front_content: When you hit 'Undo' (Ctrl+Z) in a text editor, or when you click the browser's 'Back' button, the application restores your most recent action first. Which fundamental data structure powers this behavior?
capsules.back_content: A Stack operates on a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle. You push items onto the top of the stack, and you pop items off the top of the stack, both in O(1) constant time. Accessing elements buried at the bottom is not permitted. Beyond undo history and browser back navigation, stacks power compiler syntax parsing (matching parentheses) and the CPU's own Function Call Stack managing local variables.

quiz.prompt: Which operation order governs a Stack data structure?
quiz.option_a: First-In, First-Out (FIFO)
quiz.option_b: Last-In, First-Out (LIFO)
quiz.option_c: Random-In, Random-Out
quiz.option_d: Lowest-Value, First-Out
quiz.explanation: Stacks follow LIFO: the last element added is the first one removed.
quiz.kids_hint: Think of a stack of clean plates: the last plate you place on the top of the pile is the first plate someone picks up to eat dinner!

capsules.title: Queues: First-In, First-Out (FIFO) Buffers
capsules.front_content: When 100 people send documents to an office printer at the same time, or when a web server receives thousands of simultaneous requests, how does the system process tasks fairly without dropping anyone's work?
capsules.back_content: A Queue operates on a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) principle. Tasks enqueue (join the line) at the back, and dequeue (get processed) from the front in O(1) time. Queues act as shock absorbers between fast producers and slower consumers. In web architecture, message brokers (like Celery, Redis, RabbitMQ) use queues to process background jobs like video transcoding, email delivery, and payment verification asynchronously.

quiz.prompt: What data structure is optimal for handling tasks in the exact chronological order in which they were submitted?
quiz.option_a: Stack
quiz.option_b: Queue (FIFO)
quiz.option_c: Binary Tree
quiz.option_d: Hash Set
quiz.explanation: A queue guarantees First-In, First-Out fairness: the earliest submitted task is the first to be processed.
quiz.kids_hint: Standing in line for movie tickets! Whoever gets in line first gets their ticket first.

capsules.title: Hash Tables & Collision Resolution
capsules.front_content: Hash tables (Python dicts, JavaScript objects) are the unsung heroes of software engineering. They enable instant O(1) lookups across millions of keys. But what happens when two completely different keys produce the exact same mathematical hash number?
capsules.back_content: A Hash Function converts an arbitrary key (like 'anaya@email.com') into an array index. When two keys map to the same bucket, a Collision occurs. Hash tables resolve collisions through: 1. Chaining (each bucket holds a linked list of collided key-value pairs). 2. Open Addressing (probing for the next open slot). A good hash function distributes keys uniformly to keep buckets shallow, maintaining blistering O(1) average performance.

quiz.prompt: What is a 'hash collision' in a hash table data structure?
quiz.option_a: When the computer runs out of hard drive space
quiz.option_b: When two distinct keys are evaluated by the hash function to the same array index bucket
quiz.option_c: When a key is deleted while being read
quiz.option_d: When two threads write at the exact same clock cycle
quiz.explanation: A collision occurs when distinct inputs yield the same hash value, requiring collision resolution techniques like separate chaining or linear probing.
quiz.kids_hint: Two kids arriving at the bowling alley and being assigned the exact same locker number! The locker attendant gives the second kid a little basket right next to it.

capsules.title: Binary Search Trees: Ordered Fast Lookups
capsules.front_content: If you want to maintain a collection of numbers that supports both fast lookups AND fast retrieval of items in sorted order, arrays and hash tables fall short. Hash tables cannot easily answer: 'Find the closest value below 50'. What hierarchical data structure solves this?
capsules.back_content: A Binary Search Tree (BST) organizes nodes hierarchically. The BST Invariant: for any node, all values in its left subtree are smaller, and all values in its right subtree are larger. When searching, you compare with the root: if smaller, go left; if larger, go right. Each step cuts the remaining search space in half, achieving O(log n) time. Self-balancing trees (like Red-Black trees and AVL trees) prevent trees from degrading into linear sticks.

quiz.prompt: In a valid Binary Search Tree (BST), where are values strictly less than the root node located?
quiz.option_a: In the right subtree
quiz.option_b: In the left subtree
quiz.option_c: Scattered randomly across leaf nodes
quiz.option_d: At the very top of the tree above the root
quiz.explanation: By definition, the binary search tree property requires all keys in the left subtree to be strictly less than the node's key.
quiz.kids_hint: At every branch in the tree: if the secret number is smaller, take the left path; if it's bigger, take the right path!

capsules.title: Graph Representations: Adjacency Lists vs Matrices
capsules.front_content: How does Google Maps represent roads connecting cities? How does Facebook represent friendships between 2 billion people? These networks are Graphs—collections of Vertices (nodes) connected by Edges. How does a computer store a graph in memory?
capsules.back_content: Graphs are stored primarily via: 1. Adjacency Matrix: a 2D V x V grid of 1s and 0s indicating whether an edge exists between vertex A and vertex B. Excellent for dense graphs with O(1) edge lookup, but wastes massive O(V^2) memory for sparse networks. 2. Adjacency List: each vertex maintains a list of only its directly connected neighbors. Highly memory-efficient for real-world sparse graphs like social networks, taking O(V + E) space.

quiz.prompt: Why is an Adjacency List preferred over an Adjacency Matrix for modeling a social network of millions of users?
quiz.option_a: Because social networks have only 2 users
quiz.option_b: Because real-world social graphs are sparse; each user connects to only a few hundred friends, making an adjacency matrix wasteful with millions of empty cells
quiz.option_c: Because adjacency lists are incompatible with internet protocols
quiz.option_d: Because adjacency lists prevent user account deletions
quiz.explanation: In a social network with 1,000,000 users, an adjacency matrix requires 1,000,000,000,000 cells (terabytes), whereas an adjacency list stores only actual active friendships.
quiz.kids_hint: Instead of building a giant chart with every kid in school and drawing mostly empty zeroes, you just write down your personal circle of friends!

capsules.title: Recursion & The Call Stack
capsules.front_content: In Russian Matryoshka nesting dolls, you open a doll to find a smaller doll inside, which holds an even smaller doll, until you reach the final solid figurine. Recursion in programming is a function that calls itself to solve smaller sub-problems. When does recursion become dangerous?
capsules.back_content: Every recursive function requires two parts: 1. Base Case (the stopping condition that returns directly). 2. Recursive Step (calling itself with smaller input). Each recursive call pushes a new frame onto the CPU call stack. If you forget the base case, the function calls itself indefinitely until memory exhausts, crashing with a 'RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded' (Stack Overflow). Recursion elegantly solves tree traversals and divide-and-conquer problems.

quiz.prompt: What essential component must every recursive function have to prevent infinite recursion and stack overflow crashes?
quiz.option_a: A while loop
quiz.option_b: A base case (termination condition)
quiz.option_c: A database connection
quiz.option_d: An asynchronous fetch statement
quiz.explanation: The base case provides the termination condition that returns a value without making further recursive calls, unwinding the call stack safely.
quiz.kids_hint: You must have the smallest baby doll at the very center—if the nesting dolls never ended, you'd be opening dolls forever!

capsules.title: Divide & Conquer: The Magic of Merge Sort
capsules.front_content: Sorting a messy list of 1,000,000 numbers using Bubble Sort (swapping adjacent pairs) takes roughly 1,000,000,000,000 steps—hours of computation. Yet Merge Sort sorts the identical list in under 1 second using just 20,000,000 steps. What makes Divide & Conquer so blisteringly fast?
capsules.back_content: Merge Sort applies Divide and Conquer: 1. Divide: recursively split the unsorted list in half until you have single-element sub-lists (which are inherently sorted). 2. Conquer & Combine: merge pairs of sorted sub-lists back together by comparing front elements in O(n) linear time. Splitting takes log2(n) levels, and merging each level takes O(n), guaranteeing an optimal O(n log n) runtime under all circumstances. It is the gold standard for reliable, guaranteed-performance sorting.

quiz.prompt: What is the guaranteed worst-case time complexity of Merge Sort?
quiz.option_b: O(n log n)
quiz.option_d: O(n!)
quiz.explanation: Merge sort divides the problem logarithmically (log n depth) and merges in linear time (n work per level), providing guaranteed O(n log n) efficiency even on worst-case inputs.
quiz.kids_hint: Instead of sorting a messy pile of 100 cards all at once, split them into two small piles of 50, sort each half with a friend, and zip the two neat piles together!
